tagline: Seven thousand islands in the Pacific
overview:
The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands in Southeast Asia, strung between the South China Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Only about 2,000 of the islands are inhabited, and the three biggest groups are Luzon in the north, the Visayas in the middle and Mindanao in the south. Together they cover about 342,000 km², a little larger than Italy.

About 115 million people live in the Philippines, speaking Filipino, which is based on Tagalog, and English, both official, plus more than 100 other languages including Cebuano and Ilocano. Manila, on Luzon, is the capital and the center of a metropolitan area of well over 13 million people.

The Philippines is a presidential republic and one of the two mainly Catholic countries in Asia. Millions of Filipinos work abroad as nurses, sailors and engineers, and the money they send home is a pillar of the economy.
landAndNature: The islands sit on the Ring of Fire, so volcanoes and earthquakes shape the land. Mayon volcano has an almost perfect cone; Taal is a volcano on an island in a lake on an island. Off the east coast lies the Philippine Trench, plunging more than 10,000 meters. The country lies in the path of about twenty typhoons a year, more than almost anywhere else. Rice terraces carved into the Cordillera mountains by the Ifugao 2,000 years ago climb like green staircases. The seas here hold more coral and fish species than anywhere else on Earth, part of the Coral Triangle. Tarsiers, palm-sized primates with enormous eyes, cling to branches in Bohol, and the Philippine eagle, one of the largest eagles alive, hunts in Mindanao's forests.
peopleAndCulture: Filipino life revolves around family, food and hospitality. Adobo, meat simmered in vinegar, soy sauce and garlic, is the best-known dish, alongside sinigang sour soup, lechon roast pig and halo-halo, a heaped dessert of shaved ice, sweet beans, fruit and ice cream. Jeepneys, brightly painted buses built from stretched jeep bodies, carry passengers along shared routes. Basketball is played on every village court, and boxer Manny Pacquiao became a national hero. Christmas celebrations start in September and run into January, the longest in the world, with star-shaped parol lanterns in every window. Karaoke is a beloved pastime, and the bamboo dance tinikling has dancers hopping between clapping poles.
history: People have lived in the islands for tens of thousands of years, trading with China and Southeast Asia and organized into small states called barangays; Islam spread in the south from the 1300s. Ferdinand Magellan reached the islands in 1521 and was killed by Lapu-Lapu's warriors on Mactan. Spain colonized the archipelago from 1565 and ruled for over 300 years, converting most people to Catholicism and naming the islands after King Philip II. A revolution began in 1896, and independence was declared in 1898, but the United States took control after the Spanish-American War, and a bitter Philippine-American War followed. Japan occupied the islands in World War II. Full independence came on July 4, 1946. Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law until the peaceful People Power revolution removed him in 1986.
funFacts: The Philippines has the world's longest Christmas season, with carols and decorations appearing as early as September.
Jeepneys began as surplus American army jeeps left after World War II, lengthened and decorated by local builders.
The Philippine tarsier weighs about as much as a deck of cards, and each of its eyes is bigger than its brain.
A whale shark, the world's largest fish, can be seen feeding off Philippine coasts, where it is called butanding.
The underground Puerto Princesa river flows for more than 8 kilometers through a cave straight into the sea.
